title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within‑task experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) to measure whether embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) loop increases detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated device configurations and improves bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation. Using a synthetic intent→configuration suite (N=270 tasks), gpt-5-mini as generator, a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet validator/emulator as ground truth, and preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, every generated candidate was verifier‑acceptable: baseline accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded (verify → optional bounded repair) accepted 270/270 (100%); no repairs invoked. Paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap_resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). This provenance‑anchored null arises from the executed generation semantics (one shared candidate per pair); we release the complete preregistration and execution bundle (preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d5667..., master prompt archive provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96...) and provide an artifact‑grounded recipe to run the independent‑sampling variant required to test the original estimand.

sections.introduction: LLM‑based intent→configuration pipelines promise operational efficiency in NetOps but raise safety/reliability concerns because stochastic token sampling can produce commands that are syntactically plausible yet semantically unsafe. A common mitigation pattern is Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR): (G) generate candidate configuration(s); (V) deterministically verify candidate correctness/safety with an oracle/verifier; (R) use verifier diagnostics to guide a bounded repair loop. We preregistered a paired within‑task experiment to answer the research question: does embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM GVR loop increase the proportion of unsafe or incorrect generated configurations that are detected/rejected and, if rejected, does a bounded repair loop recover verifier‑accepted outputs more often than single‑shot generation? Contributions: (1) A fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired study with complete per‑artifact SHA‑256 provenance (preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d5667...; master prompt archive SHA‑256 1872df1e...). (2) A transparent execution bundle including raw model traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, and analysis artifacts (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 43381c4b...). (3) A concrete, artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the executed run produced a degenerate null result and a minimal reproducible recipe (exact JSON field names and artifact paths) for a follow‑up that validly tests the original estimand under independent per‑arm sampling.
sections.related_work: Architectural and empirical prior work motivates GVR and verifier‑anchored pipelines for reducing hallucination and enforcing formal correctness in safety‑sensitive domains (e.g., Cadenas, Convergent Correctness; doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899). Formal network verification frameworks (NetKAT / weighted NetKAT) and automated decision procedures provide deterministic oracles suitable for insertion as V in GVR (Suárez Acevedo et al.; doi:10.1145/3808318). Recent intent‑and‑LLM NetOps system proposals document architectures combining RAG, orchestration, and verifier anchoring (sample leads archived in the evidence bundle; OpenAlex records W4414359351, W4400072049, W4386722061). Our experiment differs by preregistering a specific estimand, freezing generation/repair budgets, deterministically logging every provider call and validator trace, and releasing full artifact hashes so the exact run is reproducible.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan. The preregistered study (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; preregistration JSON SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d5667...) fixed the estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), task bank, generator family, verifier, metrics, retry policy, and repair budget. Key registered configuration fields (present in the preregistration and execution manifest) that determine sampling semantics: execution_contract.independent_condition_generation (boolean) and execution_contract.initial_generation_calls_per_task. The executed run set independent_condition_generation=false (shared_initial_candidate semantics), initial_generation_calls_per_task=1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1; these exact fields and values are recorded in execution/execution_manifest.json and the preregistration. Task bank and emulator. SyntheticNetOpsIntentConfig_v1: 270 tasks = 3 vendor‑style syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks; a 20% stratified validation subset (54 tasks) reserved for verifier↔emulator concordance checking (preregistered sampling_plan). Each task includes an intent, required_sequence, explicit allowed_touched_fields, and initial/expected final states; representative task manifests and their SHA‑256s are available under execution/task_manifest.jsonl (examples: task-000001 manifest and responses; see artifact table). Generator and model configuration. Declared generator: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...). Execution used a single shared generated candidate per paired task (shared_initial_candidate) as preregistered; model_calls_used recorded=270 (execution manifest). Verifier and validation. Deterministic_netops_validator_v5 executed against a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet emulator (emulator ground truth) served as the definitive oracle; each scoring JSON (execution/scoring/*.json) contains the validator_trace with normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, touched_field_count, violation codes, and validity. Scoring rule: full_intent_constraint_validation. Retry and failure rules. Provider/API call failures: preregistered deterministic retry policy ≤2 retries per failed call; in this execution failed_hosted_model_call_event_count=0. Guarded repair loop. Guarded arm: if verifier rejects, invoke bounded repair loop with at most one repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1). All repair prompts, provider traces, and repair outputs (if any) are archived; no repairs were invoked in this run. Statistical analysis. Primary test: paired binary comparison (exact McNemar two‑sided) and paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed=1729). The analysis executor and log are archived (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 feec505f...). Deterministic accounting. The execution manifest and per‑artifact SHA‑256 manifest record complete provenance (execution/execution_manifest.json; exemplar hashes in the manuscript bundle).

The reserved 54‑task validation subset showed verifier↔emulator agreement 54/54 (verifier false_accept=0, false_reject=0) as recorded in scoring JSONs for those episodes. Statistical inference. The degenerate CI and p value are arithmetic consequences of zero discordant pairs (n10=n01=0) under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics; they therefore do not provide evidence that verifier insertion is useless generally—rather they quantify the observed outcome conditional on identical generated candidates across arms. sections.discussion: Why the provenance‑backed null occurred. Two preregistered, archived choices explain the degenerate result: (1) execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=false (shared_initial_candidate semantics) produced a single generated candidate per task that was evaluated in both arms; (2) the chosen generator settings (gpt-5-mini per execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...) and prompt produced verifier‑acceptable outputs for every task in the synthetic suite. Both facts are recorded and verifiable in execution/execution_manifest.json and the raw response files. Consequences for estimand, power, and interpretation. The preregistered power/MDE reasoning assumed independent sampling per arm (independent_condition_generation=true). Because the executed run used shared candidates, those MDE/power assumptions do not apply and the observed p=1.0 and CI=[0.00,0.00] are degenerate. Interpretation: the result documents a conditional boundary case—when a generator (with the specified prompt/settings) produces verifier‑acceptable outputs for the test bank and a single generated candidate is used for both arms, inserting a deterministic verifier and a bounded single‑attempt repair loop will not change observed accept/reject outcomes. This is an operationally useful observation (it highlights the decisive role of generation semantics) but does not generalize to other sampling regimes, models, or verifier rule sets. Reproducible minimal follow‑up recipe (artifact‑grounded). To test the originally preregistered estimand under independent sampling, change these preregistered JSON fields and re‑run the archived harness: (A) set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=true; (B) set execution_contract.initial_generation_calls_per_task=2 (or set maximum_model_calls≥540) so each arm receives an independent generation; (C) set execution/model_configuration.json.temperature>0 or provide deterministic per‑episode seeds in task_manifest.json to expose sampling variance; (D) optionally set maximum_repair_calls_per_task>1 to probe bounded repair convergence. All field names and manifest paths referenced here are present in the archived preregistration and execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json SHA‑256 listed in the artifact bundle). Operational implications. For deployments: (i) a reliable deterministic verifier with low false_accept/false_reject against an accurate emulator can be a strong safety anchor—however, its measurable benefit depends on generator failure rate and endpoint sampling semantics; (ii) test harness designers must carefully choose generation semantics (shared vs independent sampling) to match the estimand of interest; (iii) bounded repair budgets should be matched to verifier diagnostic granularity. Reproducibility and transparency. We release the complete execution and analysis artifacts with per‑artifact SHA‑256s (execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/*). Example accessible artifacts: execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 43381c4b07e1ffab..., execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2..., analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 62cd99d7.... The initial master prompt archive is included (provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e...).
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired study integrating a deterministic network verifier into an LLM GVR pipeline and released the full provenance bundle. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and the chosen generator/settings the single generated candidate per task was verifier‑acceptable for all N=270 tasks; the verifier/repair path was therefore not invoked and the observed paired difference is exactly 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00], McNemar p=1.0). The primary scientific outcome is methodological: generation semantics (shared candidate vs independent sampling) and the generator failure rate determine whether a verifier insertion is empirically testable under the original estimand. We publish the exact artifacts and an artifact‑grounded minimal recipe (JSON fields and paths) so researchers can deterministically run the independent‑sampling variant that validly tests the original preregistered estimand.

limitations: Synthetic task suite and limited operational realism: results may not generalize to complex, noisy, adversarial, or production NetOps environments; emulator behavior can differ from heterogeneous production devices.
Single‑model evaluation: only a single generator (gpt-5-mini) was used; no claim of multi‑model generality should be inferred.

Generation semantics constraint: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced one generated candidate per task and thereby eliminated between‑arm stochastic sampling variance; the preregistered MDE calculations assumed independent sampling and are therefore inapplicable to the observed contingency.

Bounded repair budget: the repair loop allowed at most one repair call per rejected candidate (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1); multi‑attempt repair strategies were not evaluated and could change outcomes.

Verifier rule‑set sensitivity: a single deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and rule set were used; different verifier conservatism or policy choices will change false‑accept/reject tradeoffs.
Emulator vs production gap: emulator‑validated safety does not guarantee identical behavior on production devices or multi‑vendor deployments.
